steps.html:
Two people describe photographs to each other, neither of whom can see the other's. It takes them four minutes to establish that one of the markets is floating on a river — and the phrases they use to get there are the whole point of the lesson.

  • Follow two people establishing what they are talking about
  • Check, clarify and repair a misunderstanding
  • Watch an interview about how we see colour
  • Write a detailed description of a scene

steps.title: Before you listen: two people are describing photographs they cannot both see.
steps.sub: What will they need to establish first?

steps.title: Listen to the first part and answer.
steps.prompt: What is in both photographs?
steps.answer: A market
steps.why: Both are markets, which is why the difference takes so long to find.

steps.title: Listen to the first part and answer.
steps.prompt: What is the first difference they establish?
options: One photograph has a man cooking; the other has no men at all.
One is in colour and one is not.
steps.answer: One photograph has a man cooking; the other has no men at all.
steps.why: 'That's a difference, then.'

steps.title: Listen to the first part and answer.
steps.prompt: What are the sellers in the second photograph wearing?
options: Headscarves, straw hats and brightly coloured dresses.
Uniforms, which is how you can tell they work for the market.
Nothing is described — the speaker cannot make out what they wear.
steps.answer: Headscarves, straw hats and brightly coloured dresses.
steps.why: And the first speaker's photograph has nobody in a hat or a headscarf.

steps.title: Listen to the second part and answer.
steps.prompt: What is being sold in both photographs?
options: Fruit and vegetables, including a lot of bananas.
Fish, most of it laid out on ice at the front
Clothes, hung on rails behind each of the stalls
steps.answer: Fruit and vegetables, including a lot of bananas.
steps.why: Which is another similarity, not a difference.

steps.title: Listen to the second part and answer.
steps.prompt: What is the crucial difference?
options: One market is on the water — the sellers are in boats.
steps.answer: One market is on the water — the sellers are in boats.
steps.why: A floating market.

steps.title: Listen to the second part and answer.
steps.prompt: How is the misunderstanding repaired?
options: The second speaker rephrases: 'I mean they're in boats.'
They start again from the beginning.
steps.answer: The second speaker rephrases: 'I mean they're in boats.'
steps.why: After 'I'm not quite sure what you mean by on the water'.

steps.title: Language noticing.
steps.sub: 'I'm not quite sure what you mean by "on the water".'
steps.prompt: Why is this better than 'I don't understand'?
options: It is shorter, and takes less time to say out loud.
It names the exact phrase, so the other person repairs only that.
It is more formal, which suits a conversation with a stranger.
steps.answer: It names the exact phrase, so the other person repairs only that.
steps.why: The speaker then rephrases three words instead of the whole description. That is the entire technique.

steps.title: Where things are, and how you say you can see them
steps.html:
Recycled: adjective order from Lesson 41 and the sense verbs from Lesson 43, put to work.

A description needs a route through the picture. English uses a standard set of position phrases: in the foreground, in the background, in the middle distance, on the left, on the right, at the top, at the bottom, behind, in front of, half hidden by.

Introduce things with there is / there are, then describe them: There's a man in the foreground cooking something. Do not start every sentence with I can see.

When you do use a sense verb, choose it properly. I can see = it is there. It looks like / it looks as if = your interpretation. It appears that = more cautious still. It looks as if the boat is about to crash is honest; the boat is about to crash is not, because it is a painting.

Adjective order from Lesson 41 applies throughout: a small yellow and orange rubber boat, a large decorative painting, brightly coloured floral dresses.

And hedge what you cannot be sure of: I think, it seems to be, possibly, something like, a kind of. They're sitting on what looks like a rubber boat.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Ten sentences from the recording and the unit.

There's a man in the foreground cooking something.
Introduce, then place, then describe.

I can't see anyone cooking anything.
Negative of what is actually there.

They're wearing headscarves, or straw hats and brightly coloured dresses.
Hedging an uncertain detail.

My photo shows some different fruit and vegetables.
Show avoids repeating I can see.

They're sitting on what looks like a small rubber boat.
Hedged, because it may not be one.

It appears that the boat is being swept along.
Cautious interpretation.

It looks as if he's on a tiny ledge at the top of a burning building.
Interpretation, not fact.

a panther half hidden by leaves
Partial view.

the sky in the background is dark and threatening
Position, then two adjectives of the same type.

So, they're the same in that it's a market, and different in that …
Summarising a comparison.

steps.title: Describing one corner of a picture
steps.html:
1. The facts: a black cat, partly behind leaves, near the front, appearing about to jump.
  2. Introduce and place it: In the foreground there is a black panther. Not I can see a black panther — save the sense verbs.
  3. Add the partial view: …half hidden by a screen of leaves.
  4. Now interpret, and mark it as interpretation: It looks as if it is about to pounce. You do not know that; you are reading it from the posture.
  5. Check the adjective order if you add more: a large black jungle panther — size, colour, then the noun-like modifier. And hedge if you are unsure: what looks like a panther.

steps.title: Why We See Colour
steps.sub: Why We See Colour. About seven minutes.

steps.title: Answer the questions about the interview.
steps.prompt: Why does he say he studies colour?
options: Because colour is the part of perception people find beautiful.
Because it is the simplest thing the brain does, so the principles should hold everywhere else.
Because almost nobody else in the field is working on it.
steps.answer: Because it is the simplest thing the brain does, so the principles should hold everywhere else.
steps.why: 'Even jellyfish see lightness, and they don't even have a brain.'

steps.title: Answer the questions about the interview.
steps.prompt: What does he say about how we see?
options: We understand it well, and have done since the 1960s.
We do not know — and one reason is that we have been asking the wrong questions.
Only the eye matters, and the brain simply receives the image.
steps.answer: We do not know — and one reason is that we have been asking the wrong questions.
steps.why: The assumption that the brain evolved to see the world as it really is defines the questions asked.

steps.title: Answer the questions about the interview.
steps.prompt: What is colour for, in his account?
options: Distinguishing between surfaces that reflect the same amount of light but different qualities of light.
Making the world attractive enough to pay attention to.
Recognising faces, which is what the brain evolved to do first.
steps.answer: Distinguishing between surfaces that reflect the same amount of light but different qualities of light.
steps.why: Without colour, two such surfaces would look identical in lightness.

steps.title: Answer the questions about the interview.
steps.prompt: How many colour categories does he say there are?
steps.answer: Four
steps.why: Red, green, blue and yellow. Everything else is a combination — and nobody knows why four.

steps.title: Read between the lines.
steps.prompt: He says the practical outcome of his work is 'this conversation'. What does he mean?
options: The research has no application outside the laboratory.
Getting people to see that their assumptions shape their questions is itself the application.
He is more interested in publicity than in the work itself.
steps.answer: Getting people to see that their assumptions shape their questions is itself the application.
steps.why: He goes on to say that the same principles apply to how people make decisions.

steps.title: Write a detailed description of a scene.
steps.sub: 160–190 words. Describe a photograph, a painting or a view from a window so precisely that a reader could draw it. Mark every interpretation as an interpretation.
steps.html:
• Start in the foreground and work back.
  • Use <i>there is / there are</i> to introduce, not <i>I can see</i>.
  • Use <i>half hidden by</i> or <i>behind</i> at least once.
  • Mark every interpretation with <i>it looks as if</i> or <i>it appears that</i>.
  • Hedge anything you cannot make out.

Useful language

  • In the foreground there is …
  • Behind it, in the middle distance, …
  • … , half hidden by …
  • It looks as if / It appears that …
  • They're sitting on what looks like …
  • The one thing I cannot make out is …
steps.modelHtml:
The photograph on my kitchen wall

In the foreground there is a woman in her sixties, sitting on a low wooden bench with a large enamel bowl on her knees. She is shelling something — beans, I think, though the photograph is not sharp enough to be certain.

Behind her, in the middle distance, three children are running away from the camera towards a line of poplars. Only one of them is looking back. The light is coming from the left, low and yellow, so it appears to be late afternoon in early autumn.

At the top of the frame, half hidden by the trees, there is a roof with a television aerial on it, which is the only thing in the picture that dates it at all.

Nobody is posing. It looks as if the photographer said something a second before, because the woman is halfway through smiling and has not stopped shelling.
